episodes.168538: Ahead of a frontal boundary, a line of thunderstorms crossed through the Ohio Valley during the late afternoon of June 13th, moving into West Virginia during the evening hours. Hot temperatures during the day aided with providing plenty of afternoon heating for these storms to thrive as the system crossed through the region. Damaging winds were the main concern with this line of storms as it persisted across the Ohio Valley, however frequent lightning also accompanied these storms.||As this first line was exiting along southern West Virginia, a second line of storms formed along the lingering frontal boundary and pushed into the northern portion of the region during the night of the 13th. Damaging winds were again the main threat with this secondary line of storms. Following this line, yet another round of storms with damaging winds entered along the northwestern portions of the area during the early morning of June 14th as enough instability continued to be present across the area. A fourth line then passed through by the later morning hours of the 14th. ||The main impacts from these storms were the numerous trees and power lines that were blown down across the region. Multiple power outages occurred across West Virginia as a result.||Following the multiple rounds of storms, rises occurred on a few rivers across the forecast area. Isolated high water issues occurred along local roadways in Randolph and Harrison Counties, with a few roads becoming impassable for a brief period of time.
episodes.168544: A surface boundary associated with the remnants of a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) that moved across the Midwest the previous afternoon and evening, and across the Central Appalachians and into W NC overnight, moved south through the region and provided a focus for scattered severe thunderstorms during the morning to midday hours.

episodes.168584: Ahead of a frontal boundary, a line of thunderstorms crossed through the Ohio Valley during the late afternoon of June 13th, moving into northeast Kentucky during the evening hours. Hot temperatures during the day aided with providing plenty of afternoon heating for these storms to continue to develop and persist as the system crossed through the region. Damaging winds were the main concern with this line of storms as it persisted across the Ohio Valley, however frequent lightning also accompanied the storms.||A second line of storms formed along the lingering frontal boundary and pushed through the region during the night of the 13th. episodes.168626: A volatile environment of over 4000 J/KG of SBCAPE, combined with 45 to 60 knots of effective shear set the stage for multiple rounds of thunderstorm during the afternoon and evening hours of June 13th. Initial storms remained poorly organized, but did produce sporadic wind damage or hail. More substantial thunderstorm development evolved during the evening hours in northwestern Indiana and southwestern Lower Michigan and progressed east, eventually producing several swaths of wind damage. The most intense cluster of storms evolved in Berrien county Michigan and dropped rapidly southeast impacting locations extending from South Bend to Fort Wayne. Southwestern portions of Fort Wayne suffered the greatest impacts with widespread tree and structure damage from 80 to nearly 100 mph winds.
episodes.168641: While mid-level moisture was still present across northern and central New Mexico on June 13, 2022, conditions at the surface and low-levels remained very dry. This led to another afternoon of high-based, dry thunderstorm activity where gusty and erratic downburst winds were the primary hazard. Several stations across the area measured brief wind gusts in excess of 60 mph from these dry thunderstorms.
episodes.168695: A supercell thunderstorm moved across northeast Illinois including Chicago and the western suburbs during the late afternoon and early evening of June 13th.  Widespread significant wind damage occurred in many areas and two tornadoes occurred.  Thousands of trees were damaged and hundreds of trees were snapped or uprooted.  Several houses were damaged, some significantly, by falling trees.  Numerous vehicles were damaged or crushed by falling trees or tree limbs.
episodes.168696: A supercell thunderstorm which formed over northeast Illinois moved across northwest Indiana during the evening of June 13th producing localized wind damage and large hail.
episodes.168699: A supercell thunderstorm produced severe winds across parts of far southern Lake Michigan during the late afternoon and early evening of June 13th.
episodes.168703: A new mesoscale convective system (MCS) developed from the outflow of a previously mature MCS in southern Wisconsin before venturing southeast into the Ohio River Valley the evening of June 13th. Strong winds from Indiana to eastern Ohio were measured and observed; the Fort Wayne International Airport in the state of Indiana measured a wind gust of 98mph. ||The county that was hit the hardest was Tuscarawas, as a rear inflow jet advances from the northwest. Drones, a damage survey team, and aerial satellite data (Sentinel 2) showed numerous swaths of tree damage in central Tuscarawas County. Isolated areas  experienced wind damage equivalent to an EF2 tornado (wind gusts up to 120mph).

episodes.168828: A long-lived supercell thunderstorm took a similar track to a storm the previous day and caused considerable damage along its track from southern Butte County to southern Meade County, northeastern Pennington County, and Haakon County. The Belle Fourche and Philip areas saw the most significant damage again. Hail near softball size and wind gusts over 80 mph damaged property, trees, crops, and caused widespread power outages.
episodes.168868: Several severe mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) passed mostly west and southwest of the eastern mid-Atlantic on June 13 and 14. The majority of severe weather associated with these systems remained over the Ohio Valley and Southeast. A couple of areas of convection did make it further east on the morning of June 14. While instability was limited due in part to unfavorable diurnal timing, a few instances of damaging winds occurred over the eastern mid-Atlantic.

episodes.168935: A remnant Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) produced localized wind damage near the Catoctin Mountain ridgeline in north-central Maryland during the early morning hours.
episodes.168938: A cluster of severe thunderstorms over West Virginia clipped Highland County in Virginia, resulting in localized wind damage around midday.
episodes.168945: Thunderstorms produced localized gale force winds over the upper Chesapeake Bay.
episodes.168977: A convective complex moved east along and north of the Ohio River during the late afternoon and early evening hours. Widespread straight line wind damage occurred with numerous wind gusts estimated to be in the 70 to 80 mph range. Over 150,000 customers were without power across southwest Ohio after the storms moved through the region.
episodes.169069: Strong heating under a ridge of high pressure set up an environment with large mixed layer convective available potential energy, large downdraft convective available potential energy, and strong low-level lapse rates supportive of damaging winds as upstream thunderstorms entered portions of southeast South Carolina.
episodes.169070: Strong heating under a ridge of high pressure set up an environment with large mixed layer convective available potential energy, large downdraft convective available potential energy, and strong low-level lapse rates supportive of damaging winds as upstream thunderstorms entered portions of southeast Georgia.
episodes.169113: A pair of convective complexes moved southeast across central Ohio during the overnight hours.
episodes.169181: A strong thunderstorm produced hail around nickel size over portions of northern Weston County.
episodes.169182: A thunderstorm briefly became severe south of Sundance, producing hail around quarter size.
episodes.169183: A severe thunderstorm tracked northeast from Wyoming across far southwestern South Dakota, producing hail larger than golf ball size across portions of western Fall River County.
episodes.169184: A thunderstorm briefly became severe over eastern Butte County, producing some hail and wind gusts over 60 mph.
episodes.169185: A long-lived supercell thunderstorm intensified as it moved northeast into southwestern South Dakota and eventually tracked into central South Dakota. Large hail and strong wind gusts accompanied the storm, with Hot Springs receiving considerable property damage from baseball sized hail.
episodes.169190: A severe thunderstorm developed over eastern Oglala Lakota County and tracked northeast into western portions of south central South Dakota. The storm produced large hail, especially in the Kadoka area, and wind gusts over 60 mph.
episodes.169488: A surface front moved little during the evening of the 13th through predawn hours on the morning of the 14th. The front remained draped southeastward from far-southwest Lower MI and far-northeast IN, through northern OH, and into southwest PA. This front separated a very warm, humid, and unstable air mass to its southwest from a cooler, drier, and stable air mass to its northeast. Two lines of multicell thunderstorms developed and evolved southeastward along this front.||The first squall line impacted far-southwestern Lake Erie during the late evening of the 13th and generated a couple of gale-force to storm-force peak convective gusts along the northwest OH shore. A second squall line affected far-western and southwestern Lake Erie during the predawn hours on the morning of the 14th and generated another gale-force peak convective gust along the northwest OH shore. Both squall lines occurred along a tight northeast-to-southwest gradient in MUCAPE accompanying the front and amidst primarily weak to moderate MUCAPE over and near western Lake Erie. These thunderstorms also took advantage of moderate DCAPE and moderate to strong effective bulk shear.
episodes.169489: A surface front moved little during the evening of the 13th through predawn hours on the morning of the 14th. The front remained draped southeastward from far-southwest Lower MI and far-northeast IN, through northern OH, and into southwest PA. This front separated a very warm, humid, and unstable air mass to its southwest from a cooler, drier, and stable air mass to its northeast. Two mesoscale convective systems (i.e. MCS's) developed and evolved southeastward along this front.||During the late evening of the 13th through first hour of the 14th, the first bowing MCS evolved southeastward across portions of northern OH and generated widespread damaging to destructive wind gusts and three QLCS tornadoes. This MCS was a true derecho. The second bowing MCS evolved southeastward across portions of northern OH and generated sporadic damaging wind gusts during the wee hours on the morning of the 14th. Both MCS's occurred along a tight northeast-to-southwest gradient in MUCAPE accompanying the front and amidst primarily moderate to strong MUCAPE. The two MCS's also took advantage of moderate DCAPE and moderate to strong effective bulk shear.
episodes.169539: Afternoon thunderstorms produce funnel cloud near Cleveland along the Peace River in Charlotte County.
episodes.169721: Periods of convective and upslope precipitation brought areal and river flooding June 11 through June 16. Rainfall of 2 to 6 inches was common for the lower elevations of Northwest Montana between June 11 and June 15. Mountain locations received up to 10 inches of moisture over the same period. River flooding continued well into late June for the Flathead River.
episodes.170050: An isolated severe storm moved southeast across Lake Michigan from near Milwaukee and produced numerous reports of large hail up to an inch in diameter and significant wind damage in the form of hundreds of downed trees, tree limbs and numerous power lines from near South Haven southeast to Vicksburg.  Damage was significant and cleanup was still occurring for nearly two weeks after the storms struck.
episodes.170182: WNW steering flow was in place with a very hot airmass across the local area with high pressure W of the region. Remnant MCS convection rotated around the periphery of the ridge to the west and enhanced convection in the evening across SE GA.
episodes.170183: WNW steering flow was aloft with a very hot airmass across the local area with high pressure W of the region. A prevailing west coast sea breeze produced a few strong storms across the area in the afternoon and early evening with an unstable airmass in place.
episodes.170217: In response to a strong north-northeastward moving low pressure system, thunderstorm developed in a favorable environment over south central South Dakota just after midnight on the 14th, and quickly became severe with large hail and straight-line wind. Winds became increasingly extreme as they tracked northeast through the early morning, peaking between 4 and 5 AM across portions of Edmunds, McPherson and Brown Counties. Two separate personal weather stations recorded 120 mph wind gusts, one to the northwest of Roscoe and the other west of Frederick. Damage was widespread, including numerous downed trees and power lines, widespread roof, outbuilding and grain bin damage, and 16 steel towers were downed about 7 miles west-southwest of Frederick, which is indicative of 130 mph wind speeds. A Presidential Disaster Declaration was requested and then granted for six counties across South Dakota, Jones and Spink among them, to help residents recover from storm damage that took place from June 11-14th. Initial estimated statewide damage to public infrastructure is assessed at 1.6 million dollars.
episodes.170230: Multiple strong to severe thunderstorms developed over Niobrara County in east-central Wyoming with up to tennis ball sized hail on the evening of the 13th.
episodes.170387: A cold front moved across Iowa overnight from the 14th to 15th of June. The week had been steamy with near record highs and high humidity, making for a highly unstable airmass with CAPE over 3000 J/kg. Storms initiated along the front in central Iowa later on June 14th, resulting in a number of hail and wind damage reports. While storms dropped below severe limits shortly after midnight, heavy rain continued as thunderstorms trained along the nearly stationary front. This resulted in localized areas received two to four plus inches of rain that flooded a few area roadways.
episodes.170579: Thunderstorms developed over eastern Montana into western North Dakota as a surface trough moved through the area. Although some large hail fell with these storms, strong wind gusts became the main impact. The strongest winds were estimated at 90 mph in and around the city of Martin in Sheridan County, where multiple large trees were uprooted, with one tree falling on a structure and damaging it. The largest reported hail also occurred in Sheridan County, which was two inches in diameter. In addition to the hail and strong winds, heavy rain fell on southeast Wells County, with the Johnson Township area south of Sykeston suffering flash flooding with almost all roads having water over portions of them.
episodes.170612: A complex of storms moved across portions of western Wisconsin during the morning and afternoon of June 13th. Runoff from these storms caused some street flooding to occur in La Crosse (La Crosse County). A small shed fire was caused by a lightning strike near Sparta (Monroe County).
episodes.170625: A cold front approaching from the Ohio River Valley descended south into the Appalachians and interacted with a very moist and unstable environment to create thunderstorms on the night of June 13. A few of these storms produced damaging winds in southwest Virginia.
episodes.170650: A deepening surface low over the Northern Plains was advecting strong warm air into the Northland throughout the day. Despite a strong cap in place, elevated storms developed over northern Minnesota during the afternoon hours. The highly unstable environment quickly saw the storms grow upscale and eventually produced damaging winds and penny sized hail.
episodes.170700: A cluster of showers and thunderstorms developed in the overnight warm advection zone ahead of an advancing cold front. Fairly prevalent warm and dry air aloft produced an environment favorable for wind gusts, some of which occurred as showers and thunderstorms weakened in the overnight hours.
episodes.170714: A unusual summer-time upper air pattern developed across the Central Gulf Coast states  with an upper high centered just north of Alabama. Several upper level impulses rotated around the eastern side of the high and produced clusters of severe storms that tracked westward across Central Alabama.
episodes.170850: A line of thunderstorms moved south across western North Carolina during the morning. A few of the storms became strong-to-severe, producing hail and damaging wind gusts.
episodes.170851: Isolated thunderstorms developed over the Georgia mountains during the evening. One of the storms produced large hail in Rabun County.
episodes.170852: A line of thunderstorms moved south into the South Carolina Piedmont during the morning. One of the storms produced brief damaging wind gusts in Chester County.
episodes.171058: Intense severe thunderstorms moved from South Dakota into Dickey County near Ellendale during the early morning hours of June 14, producing widespread wind damage along with some hail damage over portions of the southern James River Valley.|The strongest winds, estimated at 110 mph, occurred over the Ellendale area in Dickey County, where many hardwood trees were snapped and others were uprooted, some falling onto homes. Many power poles were snapped with lines torn, and homes were damaged. The strong winds continued to the north and east, with extensive tree damage occurring in LaMoure County at Dickey and Adrian, into Stutsman County near Montpelier. In addition to the damaging winds, large hail also occurred, with the largest reported hail of three inches in diameter falling over Forbes, Dickey County, causing damage to vehicles and homes.
episodes.171090: A cold front approaching from the Ohio River Valley descended south into the Appalachians and interacted with a very moist and unstable environment to create thunderstorms on the night of June 13. A few of these storms became severe producing localized damaging winds.
episodes.171100: A cold front approaching from the Ohio River Valley descended south into the Appalachians and interacted with a very moist and unstable environment to create thunderstorms on the night of June 13 and early morning June 14. A few of these storms produced damaging winds across northwest North Carolina.
episodes.171103: A weakening convective system passed over southern and central Virginia during peak diurnal heating during the afternoon on June 14, which spawned scattered thunderstorms across primarily the Southside and Piedmont areas of Virginia. A few of these storms produced damaging winds.
episodes.171274: A weakening complex of showers and storms moved southeastward into the northwest Piedmont during the early morning hours of the 14th. The complex of showers and storms began to re-intensify as it moved into the northwest Piedmont of central North Carolina and interacted with linger modest instability. The cluster product isolated wind damage in Forsyth County.
episodes.171356: A very active summer pattern resulted in numerous reports of trees and power lines down across the tri-state area.  Most of the damage occurred on June 14th as a large MCS moved south and southwestward across most of the area.

episodes.171646: Isolated severe thunderstorms moved across portions of the Devils Lake Basin during the late evening, bringing hail and gusty winds to the area.
episodes.171647: A mesoscale convective system moved into eastern North Dakota during the morning hours of June 14th, containing isolated severe thunderstorms. Hail and damaging wind gusts were reported from the Devils Lake Basin, eastward to Grand Forks, then into west-central Minnesota.

episodes.171693: There was decent low level shear and cape values of over 2500 J/kg that led to a few severe thunderstorms.
episodes.171705: A few isolated to scattered thunderstorms produced sporadic microbursts with severe wind observations.
episodes.171781: An MCS moved through from the morning into the early afternoon on June 14, producing isolated gusty winds across southeast Virginia.
episodes.171782: An MCS moved through from the morning into the early afternoon on June 14, producing scattered gusty winds across Maryland.
episodes.171783: An MCS moved through from the morning into the early afternoon on June 14, producing scattered thunderstorms with gusty winds across portions of the Chesapeake Bay.
episodes.171798: A multi-day severe weather event unfolded mid June as multiple disturbances surrounding the outer periphery of a mid level high pushed through an abnormally moist environment and highly unstable environment over the forecast area. These storms produced numerous reports of trees & powerlines down, quarter to golf ball size hail, structural damage, and isolated instances of flash flooding.

A survey of damage indicated the swath of wind damage continued southeast from Elkhart county, first impacting Syracuse then progressing SSE into North Webster and points to the southeast towards the Noble county line. Tree damage was not widespread in Syracuse, but several tree limbs and trees were noted down across the city. The winds began to accelerate further as they moved off Lake Wawasee and just east of the NWS Northern Indiana office. One of the apartment complexes at Baypoint condos suffered roof damage as the winds caught a corner of the roof that was not properly anchored, causing loss of several pieces plywood and impacting 2 apartments with mainly water damage. The noted tree damage increased on the south side of North Webster and Webster Lake. While overall wind speeds of 60 to 70 mph were estimated, pockets of locally higher gusts likely occurred.

A survey of damage from emergency management officials indicated the swath of damage from Kosciusko county persisted southeast, clipping the southwest portion of Noble county. The damage extended from south of Cromwell towards Knapp Lake, Smalley Lake and Big Lake and towards Merriam. Numerous trees were down along this path with some structure damage noted from falling trees. Outside of the falling tree related damage, some barns and homes were impacted by the actual winds with a small unattached garage, older barn and also a horse barn collapsing. Winds were estimated from 65 to 75 mph.
The public reported a shed was destroyed.

A survey of damage by emergency management officials and NWS personnel indicated numerous trees and power lines were blown down in the Tri Lakes area, especially between State Routes 9 and 109. All roads at one point were impassable due to the amount of damage. The swath of damage continued southeast through Columbia City and towards the Allen county line. A semi was reported blown off the road on US-30. Spotter estimated and measured wind speeds of 70 to 80 mph were noted in some spots, both in the Tri Lakes area as well as approaching Allen county.

The swath of damaging winds existed southeastern Whitley county and begin to intensify further, impacting the Arcola area with numerous trees, tree limbs and power lines down, some onto structures. The damage continued southeast impacting the southwest portions of Fort Wayne and surrounding areas. The hardest hit areas extended from Aboite township into Indian Village and Waynedale. Tree and tree limb damage was extensive in some areas, causing difficulties in clearing of roadways and restoration of power as numerous power lines and poles were impacted either by the winds alone or falling trees and tree limbs. The Fox Island County Park area had to be closed for an extended period due to extensive tree damage on roads and paths. A 98 mph wind gust was recorded at the Fort Wayne Regional Airport. An 89 year old female was inside her home in the 5400 block of Mason Drive when a tree crashed into her home. She was severely injured by broken glass and passed away at a local hospital despite surgery to stop the bleeding early on the morning of June 14. The fatality was compounded by first responders being unable to reach her for an extended period of time due to the extensive tree and power line debris.

A trailer was tossed approximately 30 yards. As the tornado moved southeastward, numerous trees were uprooted or snapped. When the tornado crossed Township Road 87, numerous 2x4 planks impaled the sides and roofs of structures. The tornado dissipated as it approached the intersection of Township Roads 86 and 91. Estimated peak tornadic winds were 97 mph.

Extensive damage occurred throughout the city of Ellendale and surrounding areas. In Ellendale, many hardwood trees were snapped and others were uprooted, some falling onto homes. A home had almost all the shingles and much of the sheathing torn off the roof, and the garage door was collapsed inward. Some power poles were broken in town, and several power service lines to homes were torn. South of Ellendale to the South Dakota state line, multiple power poles were snapped. At the Ellendale Cemetery, multiple hardwood and softwood trees were snapped and others were uprooted. In parts of Ellendale, ping pong ball size hail accompanied the storm.
